title: Beyond Attack-Based Accuracy: Rethinking Adversarial Robustness Evaluation Through Structural Gradient Alignment
summary: Visual adversarial robustness remains a fundamental security property as vision systems evolve from conventional classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs), with visual inputs remaining an attack surface across generations. Yet existing evaluation methods often depend on prescribed attacks, in-distribution data, extensive probing, or classifier-specific formulations, limiting external auditing of diverse models. We introduce Structural Gradient Alignment (SGA), a complementary robustness metric measuring the structural alignment between input content and objective-conditioned local model sensitivity. SGA uses a few randomly sampled, unlabeled public probes that need not follow the downstream task distribution and only one input-gradient computation per model--probe pair. Across 38 distinct DNNs, VLMs, and LVLMs, SGA produces rankings consistent with attack-based references. Without robustness references, uncalibrated SGA achieves $83.72\%$ average pairwise agreement across eight public-probe conditions, outperforming the strongest overall baseline in all eight by $9.38$ percentage points on average. With known robustness orders of anchor models, calibrated SGA increases agreement to $85.36\%$. These results demonstrate an attack-agnostic, computationally efficient robustness signal across conventional DNNs, VLMs, and autoregressive LVLMs, downstream tasks, threat norms, probe distributions, and evaluator-knowledge settings. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/azrealwang/SGA.

title: Evolutionary-based Transfer Learning for Physical Attack on End-to-End Autoencoder Communications
comment: 31 pages, 10 figures, and 4 tables. Accepted by JNCA
summary: End-to-end autoencoder communication has emerged as a promising means of achieving efficient data transmission across various domains. Nevertheless, vulnerabilities have recently been revealed in these systems by adversarial attacks, wherein malevolent entities manipulate the transmitted signals to deceive the autoencoder. This paper leverages the applications of evolutionary algorithms to solve a challenging optimization problem of launching physical attacks against end-to-end autoencoder communication. For white-box scenarios, we introduce PAGA (Physical Attack based on Genetic Algorithm), which combines a genetic algorithm with elite population initialization to craft attack signals that degrade autoencoder performance. To gauge the efficacy of these attack signals, we employ a fitness function that assesses their capacity to induce substantial reconstruction errors and misclassification rates. A Multi-Factorial version of PAGA, referred to as PAMFGA, is proposed to deal with practical scenarios where the attackers have limited knowledge about the receiver, also known as a black-box attack. Our experimental results show that the proposed attacks can substantially degrade the reliability of the considered autoencoder communication systems across the evaluated settings. This study also underscores the critical importance of incorporating security considerations into the design and implementation of end-to-end autoencoder communication systems.

title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
summary: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.

title: I2C-GRPO: Insight Importance Checklist for Reinforcement Learning in a Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow
summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for investigative tasks over incomplete evidence, such as cybersecurity alert triage, but reinforcement learning (RL) for such tasks is difficult: intermediate steps have no verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse. We propose Insight Importance Checklist (I2C)-GRPO, a checklist reward for intermediate investigation steps. For each decision point, a panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions, their atomic forensic insights are extracted, and a separate three-model ranker panel orders the insights by importance. A reward model checks which ranked insights a candidate action targets and returns their consensus-weighted coverage. Because actions are scored without being executed, the reward is a proxy for expected investigative value, and training reduces to a one-step contextual bandit over fixed investigation prefixes. From a soft-computing perspective, the reward is an additive fuzzy measure whose rank-exponent weights act as an ordered weighted averaging (OWA)-type operator; one exponent sets its orness, i.e., how strongly the reward concentrates on the top of the judges' consensus.
  We train an open-weight Qwen3-4B Triage Agent within a fixed multi-agent Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) alert-triage workflow on DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and test it on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS trace. Across three training seeds, the agent reaches a mean F1-score of 0.869, 5.9 and 9.7 points above uniform insight weights and DIVA, and a false-positive rate of 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. Within the weighting family, false positives fall only at the highest-orness weighting evaluated. All claims are limited to DDoS alert triage; the code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset will be released.

title: INC-SRv6: In-Network Route Exploration and Fast Failover Using Segment Routing Headers in Dynamic UAV Networks
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to Electronics (MDPI)
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks require a network provisioning mechanism that guarantees delivery and latency quality of service (QoS) under dynamic conditions in next-generation airborne mesh networks by continuously learning and repairing multi-hop paths under rapid link turnover without flooding the control plane. This paper presents INC-SRv6, an in-network computing routing mechanism that repurposes the IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH) and its Segments Left (SL) pointer into a self-learning, fast-failover distributed control plane. Rather than treating the SRH as a static source-committed vector, INC-SRv6 uses the active SL pointer to partition the segment list in flight: slots ahead of SL provide capacity for hop-by-hop next-hop recording, while the suffix behind SL serves as an in-band multi-destination reachability vector. Through this dual-zone header discipline, transit routers extract distance-weighted reachability updates from arriving suffixes, gate admission by single-pass confidence with bounded binary probing, advance or reverse SL deterministically, and restore pre-transmission SRH state for local failover upon link loss. Simulations across 200-node 3D UAV networks show that under high-speed flight and repeated 20% relay outages, INC-SRv6 improves packet delivery over reactive routing (92.12% versus 89.12%) while cutting 95th-percentile tail delay from 121.26 to 8.84 ms and control packets by 35.8%, with a 4-byte compact uSID stride model reducing SRv6 control bytes by over 52%.

title: Correlation distribution for a class of Niho exponents via self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and Kloosterman sums
comment: 43 pages
summary: Let $q=2^m$ for an even $m\geq 6$ and let $d=s(q-1)+1$ with $4s\equiv5\pmod{q+1}$. In this paper, the correlation distribution between a binary m-sequence of period $q^2-1$ and its $d$-decimation is considered. The cross-correlation function takes seven values $q(i-1)-1$ for $0\leq i\leq 6$, and we determine their frequencies based on the study of low-degree self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and three mixed Kloosterman sums, which are finally expressed in terms of $K_m(1)$ and $K_m(ω)$, where $K_m(\cdot)$ is the Kloomsterman sum on the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $ω$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_4$.

title: Physical-Risk-Aware Decentralized Agents for Constrained Vehicle Communications
summary: Decentralized V2X resource control is challenging because each vehicle has only local observations, while reliability depends on network-wide interactions. We develop a physical-risk-aware spatio-temporal graph attention (PA-STGAT) framework for agentic V2X control. Each vehicle perceives its local interaction graph, retains short-term temporal context, and independently selects its PC5 resource and power. Network outcomes are used during centralized training to refine the shared policy. Transmitter-specific credits map reliability failures to individual vehicles. A dual-priced graph term further converts network violations into coordination signals for discrete resource selection, with higher priority on short time-to-collision links. Experiments show higher raw-policy reliability than the tested graph-based baselines. Under filtered execution, PA-STGAT meets the nominal empirical communication requirements across all five seeds, with tradeoffs among utility, delivery reliability, resource occupancy, and filter-induced repair. Compared with GNN+MATD3, it requires fewer resource repairs but achieves lower utility and mean delivery reliability. Mechanism ablations show that removing dual-priced graph coordination causes resource-selection collapse. Density and mobility tests characterize the operating limits of empirical constraint satisfaction.

title: Admissibility-Preserving Control for Block Strict-Feedback Systems Under Time-Varying Asymmetric Actuator and State Constraints
summary: This paper addresses the tracking control of block strict-feedback nonlinear systems subject to time-varying asymmetric actuator and full state constraints. To that end, we develop a time-varying Admissibility-Preserving Control (APC) framework, in which the Admissibility-Preserving Input Realization (APIR) generates the plant input through a dynamic realization. The APIR guarantees input admissibility under the moving actuator set whenever each actuator bound contracts slower than the decay rate of the realization, and a closed-form lower bound on its gain is derived. The state constraints are handled by a logarithmic barrier coordinate at every backstepping step, with widths measured from the virtual control to the moving envelope of the corresponding state. We prove that every state lies inside its envelope, with each virtual control only required to remain inside the envelope of the next state, while the tracking error converges to zero exponentially. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed safety-critical control scheme.

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures
summary: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

title: Online Allocation with Differential Privacy
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: We study private online allocation problems, where allocation decisions must satisfy differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive user information while optimizing performance under limited resources. We first formalize differential privacy notions suited to different privacy requirements in online allocation and establish the fundamental performance limits of any algorithm under these definitions. Based on these insights, we propose PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta algorithm for online allocation, and establish sufficient conditions under which PPOA preserves Joint DP (JDP) or Local DP (LDP) while achieving asymptotically near-optimal performance. Building on these conditions, PPOA can be instantiated into a variety of concrete algorithms. In particular, we present the specific designs, which include PPOA-DMD that preserves JDP and LDP and PPOA-FTRL that preserves JDP. We analyze their performance under both adversarial and stochastic settings and characterize the fundamental trade-offs between DP and allocation performance. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed algorithms via numerical experiments on AI model routing in battery-powered edge systems.

title: uhd-rfsoc: Bringing Off-the-Shelf RFSoC Boards to Unmodified UHD Applications
summary: Next-generation wireless research relies on software-defined radios (SDRs) with more channels and larger bandwidth. The USRP family is one of the most widely used SDR platforms, and much of the wireless software ecosystem is built on top of the USRP hardware driver (UHD). However, each USRP model comes with a fixed channel count, bandwidth, and streaming capability. Off-the-shelf radio frequency system-on-chip (RFSoC) boards, on the other hand, integrate up to 16 analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and 16 digital-to-analog converters (DACs) operating at several gigasamples per second (GS/s), but existing UHD applications cannot directly use them. We present uhd-rfsoc, an open-source FPGA design and host software stack that turns these boards, including the 16-channel ZCU216 and the RFSoC 4x2, into standard UHD devices without modifying UHD. Through standard UHD calls, applications can configure the carrier frequency, channel count, the per-channel I/Q sample rate, and the wire format. uhd-rfsoc combines timestamped, flow-controlled sample transport in the FPGA with data plane development kit (DPDK) packet processing and vectorized sample conversion on x86 and Arm hosts. The built bitstreams for a number of RFSoC board configurations with varying RF data converter rates, channel counts, I/Q sample rates, and wire formats all successfully pass UHD's built-in streaming benchmarks. We further demonstrate compatibility with unmodified GNU Radio flowgraphs, a custom GPU-accelerated transceiver digital signal processing pipeline, as well as the OCUDU and Duranta 5G radio access network stacks using both software and commodity user equipment.

title: Toward the Minimal Set of Information Inequalities in Regenerating Codes: An Algebraic Approach
summary: Information-theoretic outer bounds for exact-repair regenerating codes can be formulated as linear programs, but the associated Shannon-type systems contain many implicit equalities and redundant inequalities. We directly specify a reduced system for the $(n,n-1,n-1)$ exact-repair model using the closure structure induced by its repair dependencies. Nonempty closed sets index the reduced joint-entropy coordinates, and inseparable edges determine the defining inequalities. We prove equivalence with the initial system by characterizing its implicit equalities and establishing sufficient redundancy criteria. We also give an algorithm that constructs the directly defined system for any $n$, count its entropy coordinates, and derive an explicitly computable upper bound on its number of inequalities. For every $n\ge2$, we prove that the reduced system has no implicit equalities and that each distinct defining inequality is nonredundant and defines a facet in the nonempty closed-set coordinate space. Exact enumerations for $n\in\{2,3,4,5\}$ verify the reported system sizes.

title: When to Move: Online Repositioning of Movable Antenna Arrays Under a Long-Term Actuation Energy Budget
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables
summary: Movable antenna (MA) arrays improve multiuser throughput by repositioning their elements, but mechanical movement reduces transmission time and consumes actuation energy. Changes in user configurations create nonuniform demand for repositioning over time, while each movement determines which positions are reachable in subsequent slots. Thus, online control must decide when to spend a limited actuation-energy budget, not only where to position the antennas. We formulate causal effective-throughput maximization under displacement-dependent movement delay, inter-slot reachability, and a long-term average actuation-energy constraint. We propose Lyapunov-based online movable-antenna repositioning (LOMA), which adjusts the price of movement through a virtual queue and solves the resulting nonconvex position problem via proximal minorization--maximization, accounting for nonsmooth movement delay and promoting sparse antenna updates. We establish monotone ascent of the smoothed per-slot objective, a finite-horizon sample-path energy bound, almost-sure long-term budget feasibility under a Gaussian fading model with bounded large-scale gains, and a state-matched throughput comparison separating temporal energy allocation from per-slot optimization error. Simulations show that LOMA concentrates actuation after intermittent user changes and improves effective throughput over optimized fixed arrays and a per-slot-budget counterpart, while continuous channel drift favors more frequent incremental repositioning. Additional simulations with pilot-based channel estimates in sparse millimeter-wave channels show that LOMA retains most of the throughput benefits of online repositioning while operating near its prescribed long-term actuation-energy budget.

title: RAZeR: Representation Aware Zonotope Reduction
summary: Reachability analysis is a popular technique for verifying the safety of a dynamical system under uncertainty, where the uncertainty is often represented by zonotopes. As the size of the zonotope representation typically grows as the reachability analysis progresses, it must be repeatedly reduced at the cost of additional conservatism. While various methods exist to reduce the size of the representation, combined advantages are not fully leveraged as only a single reduction method is typically used throughout the analysis. In this work, we show how dynamically choosing which method to use can yield significantly tighter results, thereby easing verification. This is realized by introducing a heuristic, derived from model predictive control, that accounts for upcoming propagation of the current zonotope. We argue that order reduction is not merely a post-processing step after propagation but also a pre-processing step that shapes how the zonotope evolves under the system dynamics. We evaluate our approach, RAZeR, on nonlinear benchmarks taken from the ARCH-COMP, where we demonstrate that RAZeR produces tighter zonotopes at a negligible performance overhead.

title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
summary: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.

title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
summary: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($δ$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $δ$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $α> 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(α) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $α$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(α^*)$.

title: Mobile Edge Deployment and Resource Management for Maritime Wireless Networks
comment: 12 pages, 11 figures
summary: Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) has been envisioned as one of the key technologies for supplying computation and storage resources in Internet of Vessels (IoV) networks. Due to its flexible deployment, low cost and agile maneuverability, Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) has emerged as a promising solution, to provide communication and computation services for maritime users. In this paper, we study mobile edge deployment and resource management for MEC-assisted maritime wireless networks where USVs with diverse computation resources are deployed to provide edge computing services that complement the cloud-based services. To this end, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the expected response time by jointly optimizing the deployment of mobile USVs and computation offloading decisions. To solve the mixed-integer nonlinear program problem, we propose a Dual-Layer Reinforcement Learning (DLRL) framework to attain a near-optimal solution. Specifically, a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm is designed to obtain the best USV deployment in the outer layer learning, and a Q-learning algorithm is designed to determine the best computation offloading decisions in the inner layer learning. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms some literature algorithms by effectively handling both continuous and discrete variables.

title: Wireless Node Ranking via Fourier-Driven Maximum-Likelihood Estimation (extended version)
summary:
We apply non-abelian Fourier theory to the problem of maximum-likelihood estimation of the order of a line topology, based on signal strength measurements under shadowing only. This yields up to a 60-fold speedup over standard methods for uncorrelated shadowing.
  Moreover, for correlated Gaussian shadowing with a singular covariance (e.g. the joint path-loss model), maximum-likelihood recovery is exact and independent of the shadowing variance (an infinite Le Cam threshold), which our implementation confirms for $σ/α$ as high as 7.0. The key object is the covariance's null space. Its dimension is fixed by the topology; its orientation depends on the correlation function only through the per-link variances.
  Although the mechanism formally requires an exact line, it is robust to small perturbations of the formation: an approximate kernel recovers as well as the exact one. We explore the dependence on the perturbation in detail for five nodes.

title: Brain-inspired Beam Selection for mmWave RIS Communication
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Beam selection at large passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) requires either full channel knowledge or beam training, both of which entail unwanted overhead. On the other hand, learned models that predict the optimal codeword from channels sampled at a few active elements avoid both, at the cost of energy-demanding multiply-and-accumulate operations. In this paper, we propose spiking neural network (SNN)-based beam selection for a semi-active RIS assisting a mmWave multiple-input single-output communication system. Direct and sigmoid rate coding are compared against a multi- layer perceptron (MLP) of identical architecture. Energy analysis further reveals that the input layer dominates SNN energy consumption.

title: Learning monotone game-theoretic linear MPC
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure
summary: We propose a method to learn a game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC) law by imitation from input and output data of a running multi-agent system. By interpreting the recorded inputs as the first moves of the equilibria of a game played by the agents, we learn the GT-MPC weights under hard input constraints and soft output constraints, without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. We also impose that the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem is strongly monotone, which ensures the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and, hence, that the learned GT-MPC law is well defined and can be evaluated efficiently online by variational GNE-seeking algorithms for linear-quadratic games. Moreover, strong monotonicity implies that the equilibrium is almost everywhere differentiable with respect to the references and the weights, which enables automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. In addition, we promote closed-loop stability of the unconstrained equilibrium feedback by incorporating a penalty that involves a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function. Learning a GT-MPC formulation enables us to explain the agents' objectives, reproduce their behavior in simulation in new scenarios, optimize their set-points, design mechanisms, and enforce additional constraints. A numerical example illustrates the approach.

title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
summary: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
comment: This paper appears at the Trustworthy Machine Learning Workshop (ARTMAN 2026) co-located with the IEEE Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC 2026)
summary: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.

title: Resource Management and Trajectory Optimization for UAV-IRS Assisted Maritime Edge Computing Networks
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures
summary: With the exponential growth of maritime wireless devices and the rapid development of maritime applications, traditional maritime communication networks encounter communication and computation limitations in supporting computation-intensive and latency-critical tasks. Edge computing and Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) have emerged as promising techniques to improve communication and computation services for maritime devices with limited computation capabilities and battery capacity. This paper studies an IRS Mounted on Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UIRS) assisted maritime edge computing network, in which the UIRS is deployed to assist the transmission from Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) to the edge server via Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) protocol. We propose a resource management and trajectory optimization scheme by jointly optimizing subslot duration, offloading ratios, transmit power, edge computation capability allocation, UIRS phase shifts and UIRS trajectory, aiming at minimizing the overall energy consumption. Since the non-convex nature of the optimization problem, we propose a two-layered method by decomposing the original problem into two subproblems. The top-layered subproblem is solved by the Semi-Definite Relaxation (SDR) method and the underlying-layered subproblem is solved by the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed scheme can effectively and efficiently reduce overall energy consumption.

title: Rate Optimal Streaming Codes Under an Extended Delay Profile for Three-Node Relay Networks
comment: 27 pages
summary: We study streaming codes for a three-node relay network with burst lengths $b_1,b_2$ and an end-to-end decoding delay $T$. Let $u=\max\{b_1,b_2\}$ and $v=\min\{b_1,b_2\}$, and write $T-v=pu+q$, where $T\ge u+v$ and $0\le q<u$. We develop two binary constructions, SR and SR-2, using extended delay profiles that allow the relay to forward causally invertible combinations of current and past source symbols. The SR construction attains the non-adaptive rate upper bound whenever \[ \frac{T-u-v}{2u-v}\le\left\lfloor\frac{T-u-v}{u}\right\rfloor. \] SR-2 enlarges this range under the sufficient condition \[ q(v-q)\le(p-1)u(u-v). \] These constructions complement the known divisibility and large-delay regimes. We also establish two limitations of systematic ordinary coordinate forwarding. First, it cannot attain the rate upper bound when $0<T-u-v<v$. Second, for equal burst lengths $b$, it attains the bound if and only if $b\mid(T-2b)$; a quantitative upper bound gives a strictly positive rate gap in every nondivisible case. These converses allow nonlinear components and predetermined time variation within the stated ordinary-forwarding architecture. Existing adaptive schemes for equal bursts approach the same rate upper bound asymptotically using time-varying convolutional codes and lie outside the non-adaptive setting considered here.

title: Efficient Design of Flag Sequence Sets for Delay-Doppler Estimation via Riemannian Optimization
summary: This letter investigates the design of a Flag sequence set with peak-curtain auto-ambiguity functions to enable low-complexity delay-Doppler estimation. Given the predefined Curtain sequences, the Flag sequence set design problem is formulated as the minimization of the weighted integrated masked sidelobe level. To solve this problem, we first reformulate it as an unconstrained optimization problem on the unimodular manifold. Then, a tailored unimodular manifold conjugate gradient (UM-CG) algorithm is developed. Compared with the existing define algorithm, the proposed UM-CG algorithm reduces computational and storage requirements. Moreover, the global convergence of the proposed UM-CG scheme is theoretically derived under mild conditions. Numerical results demonstrate the superior optimization performance of the proposed UM-CG algorithm and show that the designed Flag sequences exhibit nearly ideal peak-curtain properties.

title: Sub-Synchronous Control Interaction Risk of Large Data Center Loads: A Frequency-Scan Assessment with Cross-Model Validation
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures. Submitted for IEEE publications
summary: Data centers are now one of the fastest-growing loads on the bulk power system, and most of their demand reaches the grid through power converters inside uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). Whether these loads can take part in sub-synchronous control interaction (SSCI), as wind and HVDC converters do, has not been studied extensively. We examine this question with impedance-based frequency scans at the point of common coupling (PCC). Using a detailed proprietary model (INS-ISU), we scan the motor, variable-frequency-drive (VFD), lighting, and UPS-fed information-technology (IT) branches of a representative facility separately. Only the UPS in double-conversion mode shows negative resistance; it covers the whole sub-synchronous band and continues up to about 170 Hz. The other branches, and the UPS in bypass mode, stay passive. We then repeat the scans on three public models from PNNL, TAMU, and NLR. None of them shows negative resistance in bypass mode, while three of the four models do in double-conversion mode. Lowering the load from rated to light load makes the negative resistance deeper, as expected for a constant-power load, so a lightly loaded facility in double-conversion mode is the worst case. Raising the UPS DC-link capacitance pushes the negative resistance into a narrow band around the fundamental. These findings give a basis for screening data centers for SSCI during interconnection studies.

title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures
summary: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/

title: iGRAIL: Blockchain-Based Generative Federated Learning for Trustworthy Healthcare Intelligence
comment: 55 pages, 45 figures, 9 tables. Preprint
summary: Healthcare organizations collect huge amounts of patient data from clinical records, medical tests, monitoring systems, and healthcare services. Such data can underpin intelligent healthcare analytics but remains distributed across institutions and cannot be shared directly due to privacy, security, and trust concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative learning without sharing raw patient records, but the exchanged model information remains vulnerable to privacy leakage, tampering, replay, and unauthorized access. In this paper, we propose iGRAIL, a blockchain-enabled generative FL framework for trustworthy healthcare intelligence. iGRAIL combines local generative learning for data augmentation with differential privacy to protect sensitive information during local training. Model communication is secured using cryptographic mechanisms, and blockchain-based verification and smart-contract access control ensure that only authorized, authentic, fresh, and integrity-preserving updates are accepted for federated aggregation. The framework is evaluated on four healthcare datasets and compared with the conventional FL and blockchain-based FL (BC-FL) under predictive, privacy, non-IID, scalability, malicious-update, security-verification, and runtime settings. For the two large diabetes datasets, iGRAIL improves accuracy by about 5.4-5.6%, the F1-score by 14.6-16.9%, and MCC by 16.0-18.1% over the best FL or BC-FL baseline. Increasing the strength of differential privacy reduces the privacy-loss parameter $ε$ by about 72.5% for the cancer dataset and 87.5% for the diabetes dataset, with only a limited loss in prediction performance. These results indicate that iGRAIL supports secure and scalable federated computing while preserving privacy, model integrity, and controlled participation, at the cost of additional computational overhead.

title: Quantum Shock and Train-Time Constrained Quantization: A Geometric Study of Finite-Resolution Variational Quantum Circuits
summary: Finite-resolution interfaces map Variational-Circuit angle to discrete codebook. Since Pauli rotations are periodic, so Euclidean rounding may produce wrong codeword near a chart boundary; error due to coordinates alone cannot measure how much the final state was changed. Herein we define a metric, Quantum Shock, for Pure State it is defined as the average of the square of the Fubini-Study distance (over all inputs) between the pre-deployment and deployed states. This value is limited by constant multipliers of the mean of infidelity and provides upper limits on displacement when observing bounded quantities and margin based predictive stability. Extensions to the analytical Bures-angle for mixed-states were derived, along with a finite shot stability bound. The proposed Train-Time Constrained Quantization allows a delay in applying a penalty for selecting a codeword aligned with periodicity until after task only optimizations. Three small binary tasks were evaluated on a four qubit, two layer classifier using ten matched seeds, K = 4, 8, 16 and exact expectation values from simulation under noiseless conditions and state vector simulations. On our primary evaluation, T-CQ exhibited smaller average local quantum shock compared to circular post-training quantization for each task and code-book size tested. The re-execution on the x86-64 platform using K=8 preserved the direction of the mean-shock comparison but had varying magnitudes.

title: Hamming and Johnson-Type Bounds for Joint Error Correction and Detection
comment: This manuscript is a preliminary draft and is currently being revised. The final version will be posted once the revisions are complete. Comments and suggestions are welcome
summary: We derive upper bounds on the size of codes for joint error correction and detection over classical $q$-ary Hamming spaces. A $(c,c')$ joint error correcting and detecting code corrects every error of weight at most $c$ and detects every error whose weight lies between $c+1$ and $c+c'$. We establish equivalent conditions for this decoding requirement using Hamming balls and Hamming rings, and derive a joint bound that reduces to the Hamming bound when $c'=0$. We introduce joint perfect codes and show that binary repetition codes attain the joint bound whenever $n=2c+c'+1$. For codes satisfying $d_{\min}=2c+c'+1$, we investigate an alternative joint bound based on ring multiplicity and constant-weight code bounds. A further argument using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and pairwise ring intersections yields a refined joint bound that is always at least as strong as the original joint bound. We then incorporate an additional outer Hamming shell to obtain a Johnson-type extension. This extension provides a strict improvement for binary codes with $c'=1$, $d_{\min}=2c+2$, $c\geq2$, and $d_{\min}+2\leq n\leq3d_{\min}/2-1$. These results connect sphere-packing bounds with the geometry of joint error correction and detection.

title: Constant-Weight Sparse Vector Coded Augmented-AFDM
summary: Sparse vector coding (SVC) and its variants convey information through sparse vectors (SVs), or sparse support patterns and detecting information by solving sparse recovery problems, making them attractive for short-packet ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC). However, as the required information rate increases, conventional SVC schemes or the enhanced SVC (ESVC) schemes require a rapidly growing number of SVs, resulting in significant increase of complexity and receiver processing latency. On the other hand, when communicating in doubly selective channels, orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) suffers from the Doppler spread induced inter-carrier interference, while affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) experiences the same peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) problem as OFDM, although it allows diversity gain from channel's double selectivity. To address these issues, this paper proposes a constant-weight sparse vector coded augmented AFDM (CW-SVC/A$^2$FDM ) scheme, along with a corresponding joint support and symbol detection algorithm. In this scheme, SVs are represented by constant-weight codewords that feature a fixed Hamming weight and a large Hamming distance, resulting in relatively small SV sets. Simulation results compare various SVC/ESVC schemes and diverse coding schemes employed by the CW-SVC/A$^2$FDM, including Hamming, BCH, RS, and polar codes, for QAM symbol protection. The results demonstrate that the proposed scheme provides a distinct reliability advantage over conventional SVC/ESVC schemes, achieving a gain of up to 14 dB. Furthermore, the study indicates that the CWC's weight and minimum Hamming distance must be carefully selected to balance detection reliability, QAM modulation order, and sparse recovery feasibility, thereby maximizing the overall system's performance.

title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller
summary: This paper presents a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller for battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing and photovoltaic (PV) ramp-rate smoothing. Rapid PV power fluctuations caused by cloud transitions can introduce operational and stability challenges in power systems. To mitigate these impacts, grid codes impose ramp-rate limits (RRL) on PV power injected to the grid. BESSs can support such grid codes by absorbing or supplying power during rapid variations. However, the extent to which BESSs can reduce PV-induced variability depends on (i) the BESS power and energy capacities; and (ii) the adopted controller. Thus, BESS sizing and controller design are coupled. Conventional moving-average control can increase battery usage due to filter-induced lag, while ramp-rate control is reactive and does not account for the long-term impact of actions on battery state of charge and future ramp events. Optimization-based methods can reduce BESS requirements by anticipating future PV variations, but their performance depends on accurate PV forecasts. To address these limitations, the CARL controller learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without requiring forecasts during deployment. Ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge constraints are incorporated into a causal feasibility interval that guarantees feasible actions by definition. A full-horizon input-convex neural network (ICNN)-based optimization is developed as a noncausal benchmark for the minimum achievable BESS requirements. Evaluation using three real-world PV datasets shows that, at a 10\%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduces peak BESS power by 8.7--10.4\% and energy capacity by 47.5--62.6\% relative to conventional ramp-rate control while maintaining the grid-codes compliance.

title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

title: Evaluating the Robustness of PRNU Source-Camera Attribution to the Fingerprint-Copy Attack: An Open Toolkit with Triangle-Test Detection
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Toolkit: https://github.com/geradts1/forensicsd
summary: Photo-Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) is the de facto standard trace for sensor-level source-camera attribution, and a high Peak-to-Correlation-Energy (PCE) between a questioned image and a camera reference fingerprint is routinely treated as strong evidence of common origin. The fingerprint-copy attack of Goljan, Fridrich and Chen (2011) shows that this signal can be forged: an adversary who estimates a target camera's fingerprint from that camera's publicly available images can inject a scaled copy of it into an unrelated photograph, producing a forgery that clears a PCE decision threshold despite never having been taken by the target device. We present prnucf, an open, auditable toolkit that pairs a reference implementation of the (additive) fingerprint-copy attack with the triangle-test detector and a cohort-calibrated decision procedure, so that practitioners can quantify how fragile a PRNU attribution is against this attack on their own pipelines. On a controlled multi-camera Monte-Carlo benchmark the attack reaches an arbitrary target PCE at a mean PSNR of 59.2 dB (visually lossless), yet the triangle test separates forgeries from innocent images with an area under the ROC curve of 0.999, detecting every forgery at a cohort-calibrated 5% false-positive operating point. We discuss why a fixed significance cut-off is not safe in casework, the limitations of synthetic validation, and the open problem of extending explainable detection to the modern, GAN-based generation of fingerprint-transfer attacks. The toolkit is released under the MIT license with an explicit dual-use statement.

title: Space-based Zero-trust Architecture for Securing the Direct-to-Cell Paradigm
summary: The rapid evolution of Direct-to-Cell (D2C) technology has emerged as a pivotal enabler for ubiquitous 6G global coverage, seamlessly connecting massive numbers of User Equipment (UEs) in remote and underserved areas. However, by bypassing traditional terrestrial satellite access gateways, the D2C paradigm inadvertently renders conventional front-end security perimeters obsolete. Consequently, malicious UEs can directly expose satellites and their core networks to severe security vulnerabilities. To address these critical threats, this article proposes a Space-based Zero-Trust Architecture (SZTA) empowered by on-board satellite computing. Specifically, the proposed SZTA consists of three core components: radio frequency (RF) fingerprint-based authentication, distributed identity management, and behavior-driven dynamic access control. This architecture enables continuous, real-time verification of UE identity authenticity and behavioral legitimacy, effectively mitigating the inherent network-layer security risks of D2C networks. Simulation results demonstrate the robustness, effectiveness, and efficiency of the proposed SZTA. Finally, to facilitate the practical deployment of {the SZTA}, we discuss key technical challenges, propose corresponding solutions, and outline open research issues to guide future investigations.

title: Movable Antenna-Aided ISAC: A Time- and Frequency-Division Framework
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
summary: This paper investigates movable-antenna (MA)-enhanced integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) under time division duplex (TDD) and frequency division duplex (FDD) protocols, where sensing and communications occupy orthogonal time and frequency resources, respectively. A wideband target-position Cramér-Rao bound (CRB) is derived under a pulse-radar framework with pulse compression, incorporating delay and angle estimation error bounds in Cartesian coordinates. Both bounds depend on sensing power; the delay bound also depends on sensing bandwidth, while the angle bound depends on the effective aperture determined by the antenna position vector (APV). A worst-case position CRB over a prescribed target region ensures robust sensing performance. For multiuser downlink communication, joint APV and resource-allocation problems are formulated for TDD and FDD to maximize the minimum achievable user rate subject to the sensing requirement. An alternating optimization algorithm is developed for FDD, while TDD is addressed by searching over feasible sensing pulse numbers combined with APV optimization. Representative scenarios clarify how MA improves channel orthogonality and enlarges the sensing aperture, and how these effects shape the TDD/FDD rate comparison. Numerical results show that APV optimization enlarges the communication-sensing tradeoff region over fixed-position antenna benchmarks. The optimized configurations exhibit distinct tendencies: TDD favors a larger antenna position variance, whereas FDD favors better channel orthogonality among users.

title: Recursive Semi-Blind Receivers for Wideband Array Processing
summary: Using the commonly employed uniform rectangular array (URA) as an illustrative example, we have recently shown that the block-term tensor decomposition (BTD) model provides a natural representation for the output signal of a multi-dimensional separable sensor array structure in the presence of channel multipath. A palette of effective and efficient semi-blind joint channel estimation/data detection (JCD) algorithms for URA processing, which wed BTD modeling with existing JCD schemes, has thus been developed, and recently extended so as to be applicable in large-scale arrays and/or time-varying environments. However, both the model and the algorithms were based on the assumption of narrowband signals, arriving through paths of effectively the same delay. In this paper, recursive JCD algorithms for wideband sources are developed and evaluated through simulations in a time-varying setting and across different constellation sizes, in comparison with their batch counterparts and the training-only-based solution. They are seen to enjoy the ability to track channel variations and detect the transmitted symbols `on the fly', with the aid of only a short initial training stage.

title: Feasibility of Pareto-Improving Damping Control of Forced Oscillations: The Active-Power Case
summary: Damping control of a forced oscillation may reduce amplitudes at certain locations while increasing them elsewhere. This paper introduces Pareto improvement as a criterion for assessing such control: at least one nodal oscillation amplitude decreases, while none increases across all other nodes. The analysis considers active-power forcing sources and active-power control injections in connected swing networks with positive inertia and damping. Necessary conditions for Pareto improvement feasibility are derived from the normalized nodal responses. It is proven that for every network with a single oscillation source and a single actuator, at least one positive forcing frequency is shown to preclude Pareto improvement, regardless of the amplitude and phase of the control input. A three-node counterexample shows that this limitation does not persist with multiple actuators. PSS/E simulations of a 6-bus benchmark system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system validated the analysis. These findings suggest the value of assessing control effects across the network and further investigating multi-actuator damping control.

title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
summary: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

title: Inferring Sensitive Events in Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems via Scheduling Side Channels
summary: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We show that these mode changes create a timing side channel: by altering the interference experienced by co-running tasks, they let an unprivileged co-resident observer infer sensitive events, such as a homeowner's arrival or a vehicle's route, from its own execution timing and, on multicore platforms, its core assignment. Existing schedule-based attacks and defenses miss this channel because they assume single-mode systems or target a specific, known victim task. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ($ε=10$), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.

title: Starlight: Whittle-Driven Fidelity Rescue for Satellite-Terrestrial Quantum Networks
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables
summary: A planetary-scale quantum internet is constrained by exponential attenuation in terrestrial fibers. Low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites provide a low-loss vacuum backbone, but limited satellite resources must be allocated among competing connections under continuously evolving and heterogeneous physical conditions. Existing satellite scheduling remains largely provisioning-oriented, optimizing satellite-resource assignment for aggregate entanglement delivery. Recent age-based approaches instead incorporate chronological freshness into entanglement scheduling. Neither line of work directly identifies the connections most urgently requiring satellite assistance as their physical states evolve. We propose Starlight, a demand-driven satellite-terrestrial entanglement routing architecture that targets degrading connections before their terrestrial entanglement becomes unusable. Starlight introduces Effective Age of State (EAoS), a physics-aware metric that maps heterogeneous decoherence and swapping-induced fidelity penalties onto a unified additive coordinate. Representing each connection by evolving EAoS, we formulate rescue scheduling as a Restless Multi-Armed Bandit (RMAB) problem and derive a closed-form Whittle-style index approximation for top-K selection. Starlight further employs a two-timescale control plane and an asynchronous dispatch-and-mask pipeline to suppress redundant in-flight allocations. Simulations show that Starlight achieves up to 84.5% average satisfaction under constrained rescue capacity and sub-0.5-ms orchestration at 1,000 connections, while remaining robust to heterogeneous memory decay and stochastic atmospheric degradation.

title: New Results on the Subfield Metric
summary:
In this paper, we further develop the theory of the recently introduced $λ$-subfield metric. We investigate extremal codes, classical bounds and asymptotic densities in this setting.
  We first study codes attaining a Singleton-type bound, called Maximum $λ$-subfield Distance (M$λ$D) codes. We establish structural restrictions on their parameters and extend the theory to sublinear codes. We then investigate the asymptotic density of M$λ$D codes in several parameter regimes and compare their behavior with that of MDS and MRD codes.
  We then turn to a Plotkin-like bound, where we construct a family of constant-weight codes attaining the bound and classify all non-degenerate linear constant-weight codes for $λ>1$.
  Finally, we complement the collection of classical coding-theoretic bounds available for the $λ$-subfield metric by deriving Griesmer-, Elias- and Johnson-type bounds.

title: Dynamic Structural Causal Models for Delay Prediction
comment: Accepted in IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning for Communication and Networking (ICMLCN) 2026
summary: Dynamic network key performance indicators (KPIs) such as end-to-end (E2E) delay are shaped by both contemporaneous interactions and temporal persistence. While standard predictors can forecast KPIs under a fixed regime, proactive network management requires reasoning about the effects of explicit actions (interventions) and, in time series, executing a model forward over multiple horizons. We study dynamic structural causal models (DSCMs) for E2E delay in a 5G measurement campaign, where payload and background traffic are intentionally manipulated and thus treated as do-interventions. We learn DSCM scaffolds using four time-series causal discovery methods representing score-based and constraint-based paradigms and common lag-based baselines. Using gradient-boosted decision trees, we evaluate true multi-step DSCM rollout, which recursively simulates the full system state, and a direct target-only ablation that predicts the KPI without recursive simulation. Across two held-out intervention scenarios, including high payload and 10 Mbps background traffic, we find that the inferred target parent/lag sets differ substantially across methods and that rollout behavior is strongly scenario-dependent. In particular, PCMCI+ achieves the best short-horizon rollout accuracy under the payload intervention (RMSE 2.97~ms) but exhibits pronounced horizon-dependent degradation under the background-traffic intervention (root mean squared error (RMSE) ~4.75 ms for long horizon), yielding a large positive rollout tax of up to ~0.78 ms relative to direct prediction; DyNoTEARS and VAR-based DSCMs remain comparatively stable under rollout. These results highlight that evaluating causal scaffolds only via direct prediction can be misleading, and therefore, executability under intervention and long-horizon error propagation are critical for DSCM-based KPI reasoning.

title: Orbit-AWARE: From Onboard AI Deployment to Sustainable In-Orbit Intelligence
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, submitted to IEEE Wireless Communications
summary: The growing role of space computing in time-critical satellite services makes the long-term reliability of onboard artificial intelligence (AI) a mission-level requirement. Model drift can undermine this reliability through critical-observation suppression or noncritical priority flooding, displacing both mission information and evidence for model correction. To address this drift-induced evidence displacement, this article presents Orbit-AWARE, a safeguard-first lifecycle management (LCM) architecture. A comparison of existing approaches motivates cooperative Data, Cognitive, and Trust Planes for continuous monitoring, event-triggered agentic orchestration, and deterministic governance. The architecture retains a model-independent sample stream before degradation is confirmed and coordinates evidence selection and exchange for diagnosis and ground-assisted adaptation. Candidate updates are verified before control over data disposition is restored. In an xBD-based emergency Earth observation (EO) case study, Orbit-AWARE delivers 14.3\% more critical observations and achieves 8.3\% higher sustainable mission utility than the Rule-Based Drift Loop under a common 10\% downlink budget. Finally, we discuss future research directions for extending LCM through task-aware reliability assessment, memory- and tool-enabled onboard agents, and evidence-centric space networking. This work makes evidence availability and recovery authorization explicit design objectives for dependable onboard AI services.

title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
summary: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

title: LLMs are Vulnerable to Malicious Requests with Indistinguishable Intent
summary: Jailbreak attacks can circumvent the safety mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and lead to the generation of harmful or policy-violating content. We first examine eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter and observe that requests resembling normal user queries tend to have higher filter pass rates than those containing obvious anomalous patterns. This observation motivates the hypothesis that resemblance to normal requests may contribute to jailbreak success. We introduce \textbf{Detail Guidance Attack (DGA)}, a framework that uses an auxiliary LLM to construct detailed requests and interacts with the victim model in a single turn. Across 11 victim models and three datasets, the complete DGA pipeline achieves high attack success rates under our automated judging criterion, including rates above 95\% in several evaluated settings. We also evaluate a DGA-aware filter and conduct a user study on everyday requests with ambiguous or dual-use intent. The survey documents differing expectations about whether models should respond; the usability costs of the filter remain to be measured.

title: Evaluating Polling Schemes for OFDMA Uplink Scheduling in Time-Sensitive Wi-Fi Networks
summary: IEEE 802.11ax introduced orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) to improve channel utilization through concurrent multi-user transmissions. For effective uplink (UL) scheduling, the access point (AP) requires timely knowledge of buffered traffic at the stations (STAs). Explicit buffer-status polling provides this, yet each polling round can query only as many STAs as there are resource units (RUs). Scheduled-access, random-access, activity-based, and learning-based schemes address this buffer-status acquisition problem differently and have generally been evaluated in isolation under different conditions, so it remains unclear how they compare across time-sensitive workloads. We evaluate common schemes from the Wi-Fi standard and literature under three time-sensitive environments: a large-scale teleconferencing session, an industrial IoT deployment, and an extended reality (XR) service. The relative performance of the schemes depends strongly on traffic characteristics and offered load. In conferencing, activity-based and learning-based polling perform best, while conventional contention-based access remains competitive under light load. In the industrial scenario, scheduled-access most effectively delivers time-sensitive packets within their deadlines under heavy load, whereas contention-based access performs best under lighter load. In XR, OFDMA-based schemes achieve high video throughput that contention-based access cannot sustain; among them, activity-based polling achieves the lowest deadline-miss ratios for uplink head-tracking traffic, at the expense of longer video delay tails. These findings highlight the importance of selecting channel access and scheduling schemes according to traffic requirements and operating conditions.

title: Quadratic APN Functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with a Self-Equivalence of Prime Order
summary: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have the lowest possible differential uniformity. The only known APN permutation in even dimension, in dimension six, is equivalent to a quadratic APN function with a nontrivial linear self-equivalence; no APN permutation is known for even $n \geq 8$. In a published collection of about 3.8 million quadratic APN classes of dimension eight, at most 0.34% have a nontrivial linear self-equivalence. In dimension ten, the 25 literature classes considered here all have one. We study all quadratic APN functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with such a self-equivalence, which usually confines them to a much smaller linear space. Up to conjugacy and power similarity, self-equivalences of prime order have 299 types. We settle 298 of them. Elementary lemmas exclude 280 types, and exhaustive searches confirm this for 242 of them. The other 18 types are settled by exhaustive searches with exact equivalence certificates. Up to extended affine equivalence, the 298 types contain 29 classes of quadratic APN functions, four of them new. This also classifies the quadratic APN functions with coefficients in a subfield. Exactly 24 classes contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_4$, and all 3 that contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{32}$ are among them. The open type consists of the quadratic canonical triplicate functions. They correspond to maximum additive Hermitian rank-distance codes. Three different searches find only the invariants of 16 classes, all among the 29. We conjecture there are no others. No quadratic APN function in the 298 settled types is Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev equivalent to a permutation.

title: Channel Prediction Using Deep Recurrent Neural Network with EVT-based Adaptive Quantile Loss Function
comment: Published in: IEEE Communications Letters ( Volume: 29, Issue: 7, July 2025)
summary: Ultra-reliable low latency communication (URLLC) systems are pivotal for applications demanding high reliability and low latency, such as autonomous vehicles. In such contexts, channel prediction becomes essential to maintaining communication quality, as it allows the system to anticipate and mitigate the effects of fast-fading channels, thereby reducing the risk of packet loss and latency spikes. This letter presents a novel framework that integrates neural networks with extreme value theory (EVT) to enhance channel prediction, focusing on predicting extreme channel events that challenge URLLC performance. We propose an EVT-based adaptive quantile loss function that integrates EVT into the loss function of the deep recurrent neural networks (DRNNs) with gated recurrent units (GRUs) to predict extreme channel conditions efficiently. The numerical results indicate that the proposed GRU model, utilizing the EVT-based adaptive quantile loss function, significantly outperforms the traditional GRU. It predicts a tail portion of 7.26%, which closely aligns with the empirical 7.49%, while the traditional GRU model only predicts 2.4%. This demonstrates the superior capability of the proposed model in capturing tail values that are critical for URLLC systems.

title: Frequency-Security-Aware Real-Time Economic Dispatch with Data Center UPS Flexibility for Inertia and Primary Frequency Response Services
summary: The increasing penetration of renewable energy and the rapid growth of AI data centers are introducing significant challenges to power system frequency security. There is an urgent need to identify grid-compatible resources capable of providing fast frequency support. This paper proposes a frequency-security-aware real-time economic dispatch (RTED) model that enables data center (DC) uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems to provide steady-state power balancing, inertia response, and primary frequency response (PFR) services. Specifically, tractable analytical frequency-security constraints are derived and incorporated into the RTED framework through second-order cone programming (SOCP) formulation. The proposed model jointly optimizes energy, reserve, and inertia to minimize system operation cost while preventing under-frequency load shedding (UFLS). Numerical validation on a modified IEEE 39-bus system demonstrates that the proposed RTED model with UPS flexibility can economically support system operation and significantly improve frequency security under active-power deficit disturbances.

title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
comment: 23 pages, 21 figures
summary: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
summary: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness.
